title: Starmer Bows Out at Final PMQs with Tributes, Jokes, and a Standing Ovation
summary: In a rare display of parliamentary unity, outgoing UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer received a standing ovation from both sides of the House of Commons at his final Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday. Starmer, forced out by his own Labour Party just two years after a landslide victory, told MPs it was the “end of my political journey” and that he was “proud of everything I have achieved.” The 50-minute session saw normal hostilities set aside as MPs shared anecdotes and jokes—about England’s World Cup hopes and a by-election—while also paying tribute to the departing leader. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch refrained from attacking Starmer’s record, instead praising his work on Ukraine and his friendship with President Volodymyr Zelensky. Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey called him a “true patriot.” Emotion ran high on the Labour benches: Chancellor Rachel Reeves appeared close to tears, and MP Carolyn Harris choked up while lauding Starmer’s “decency and courage.” The prime minister directly addressed campaigners in the gallery, saying, “You’re the reason I came into politics.” The session began on a somber note with tributes to former MP Ann Widdecombe, and Starmer noted it was “chilling” that three MPs had been killed during his time in Parliament. Starmer will formally hand over power to Andy Burnham on Monday, after the former Greater Manchester mayor is confirmed as Labour leader at a special conference on Friday. Burnham, notably, was absent from the session—as he has been from all PMQs since returning to Parliament. For Starmer, a former top lawyer whose “Mr. Rules” approach struggled to connect with the public, the warm farewell offered a moment of personal vindication amid political defeat.
why_it_matters: The rapid downfall of a prime minister just two years after a huge election win illustrates how party loyalty and public image can matter more than raw electoral success. This matters because political instability can shift a country’s direction on issues like climate, education, and jobs, which will shape the future that today’s teens will inherit.

background_read: Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs) is a half-hour session every Wednesday when the prime minister answers questions from MPs, often with fierce debate.

Keir Starmer, a former Director of Public Prosecutions (the head of the Crown Prosecution Service), led the Labour Party to a landslide victory in the 2024 general election — a landslide means winning by a huge margin.
The House of Commons is the elected chamber of the UK Parliament, and the public gallery allows ordinary people to watch proceedings.
The loss of sitting MPs to violence — Jo Cox in 2016 and Sir David Amess in 2021 — has deeply shaken British politics and led to increased security measures.

perspectives.description: Starmer’s farewell shows that a leader can win respect across party lines for personal integrity and service, reminding us that politics doesn’t have to be purely combative.
His forced exit exposes the Labour Party’s infighting, which could undermine voter trust and the party’s ability to deliver on its promises.

Such quick turnover in prime ministers — Starmer is the third in less than five years — points to a deeper trend of fragile leadership in British politics, where internal party rebellions can oust even landslide winners.

Andy Burnham’s leadership may bring a fresh approach, but his absence from parliamentary debate raises questions about how he will engage with lawmakers and the public to push Labour’s agenda forward.
